lead: A real machine does one thing at a time. A design is easier to write if the machine may also switch state without reading a symbol. That switch is the ε-transition: an edge labelled ε that consumes no input. It lets us glue two small automata together, or drop in a sub-machine for a regular expression, without matching symbols at the joint. This chapter defines the ε-NFA, the ε-closure needed to run one, and the recipe that deletes every ε-edge without changing the language accepted.
prereq: You need: 1.4 NFA and the extended transition function from 1.3.

blocks.text: An ε-NFA is a five-tuple (Q, Σ, δ, q0, F) just like an NFA, with one change: the transition function also accepts the symbol ε.

blocks.where: Q is the finite set of states; Σ is the input alphabet; q<sub>0</sub> is the start state; F ⊆ Q is the set of final states; 2<sup>Q</sup> (the power set of Q) is the set of all subsets of Q, because δ returns a set of states, possibly empty.

blocks.text: ε is not a letter of Σ. δ(p, ε) = {q} means: while sitting in p, jump to q without looking at the input. Some syllabi call these finite automata with ε-moves.

items: Glueing: two small machines joined by one ε-edge behave as a sequence, with no need to copy states or align symbols at the joint.
Patterns: when a regular expression is turned into a machine mechanically, ε-edges let each operator be fitted on without rewriting the parts (see Unit 2).
Short descriptions: a language that needs many states without ε may need very few with it.

blocks.text: Acceptance does not change. The machine reads the whole string, may take ε-edges at any moment, and accepts if at least one run ends in F. ε-edges only add paths; they never take input away.
Before the first symbol is read, the machine is not in one state — it is in every state it can slide into for free. That set is the ε-closure.
ECLOSE(q) = { p ∈ Q | p is reachable from q by a path of ε-edges only }
blocks.where: q is a state; a path of zero edges is allowed, so q always belongs to ECLOSE(q). For a set S, ECLOSE(S) = ∪ ECLOSE(q) over all q in S.

items: Put q in a set; that is the seed.
Pick any state in the set and add every state joined to it by one ε-edge.
Repeat until no new state appears; the set is ECLOSE(q).
For a set of states, take the union of the closures of its members.

blocks.text: Closure is one-way reachability, never symmetric. In the figure, ECLOSE(q<sub>0</sub>) = {q<sub>0</sub>, q<sub>1</sub>} but ECLOSE(q<sub>1</sub>) = {q<sub>1</sub>}, because that ε-edge points from q<sub>0</sub> to q<sub>1</sub> only.
δ̂(q, ε) = ECLOSE(q)        δ̂(q, wa) = ECLOSE( ∪ δ(p, a) ) over p ∈ δ̂(q, w)
blocks.where: q is a state, w a string, a a single symbol, δ̂(q, w) the set of states reachable after reading w, and δ(p, a) the set of states reached from p by one non-ε edge labelled a. The union runs over every state p in the current set; the outer ECLOSE adds the free moves.

items: For the next symbol a, collect the a-moves out of every state in S.
Take the ε-closure of that collection; this is the new S.
Repeat for every symbol, then accept if S ∩ F is not empty.

blocks.text: L(M) = { w ∈ Σ* | δ̂(q<sub>0</sub>, w) ∩ F ≠ ∅ }
blocks.where: Σ* is the set of all strings over Σ; the condition says at least one state in the final set is accepting.

blocks.text: Any ε-NFA M = (Q, Σ, δ, q<sub>0</sub>, F) can be rewritten as an ordinary NFA M' = (Q, Σ, δ', q<sub>0</sub>, F') with no ε-edges and the same language.

items: δ'(q, a) = δ̂(q, a) for every state q and symbol a. One symbol of the new machine does the work of an ε-slide, a symbol, and another ε-slide.
F' = { q ∈ Q | ECLOSE(q) ∩ F ≠ ∅ }. A state is final in M' if the old machine could reach an old final state from it without reading input.
States and start state stay the same; only edges and finals change. δ'(q, a) may be empty.

blocks.text: The consequence is the headline result: ε-NFAs accept exactly the regular languages. They add convenience, not power. Making M' deterministic is the subset construction of 1.6.

figure.caption: The two dashed edges read nothing, so the machine starts in {q0, q1}, and the moment it reaches q2 it is also in the final q3. Reading ab therefore ends in {q2, q3} and is accepted.

spec.aria: An ε-NFA q0, q1, q2, q3 with a-loops on q0 and q3, a b-edge from q1 to q2 and dashed ε-edges q0 to q1 and q2 to q3; below, the four closures and the sets {q0, q1}, {q0, q1}, {q2, q3} while reading ab.

examples.question: The ε-NFA M in the figure has Q = {q0, q1, q2, q3}, Σ = {a, b}, start state q0, F = {q3}, and transitions δ(q0, a) = {q0}, δ(q0, ε) = {q1}, δ(q1, b) = {q2}, δ(q2, ε) = {q3}, δ(q3, a) = {q3}; every other move is empty. (a) Find all four ε-closures. (b) Compute δ̂(q0, ab) and decide whether ab ∈ L(M). (c) Build the equivalent ε-free NFA and list its final states.
steps: ECLOSE(q0): q0, plus one ε-edge q0 → q1, so {q0, q1}.
ECLOSE(q2): q2, plus one ε-edge q2 → q3, so {q2, q3}.
Read a: a-moves from q0 give q0; q1 gives nothing. Union {q0}; closure {q0, q1}.
Read b: b-moves from q0 give nothing; q1 gives q2. Union {q2}; closure {q2, q3}.
q3 ∈ F and q3 ∈ {q2, q3}, so ab is accepted.
Finals: ECLOSE(q0) misses F, ECLOSE(q1) misses F, ECLOSE(q2) meets F, ECLOSE(q3) meets F. Hence F' = {q2, q3}.
examples.answer: δ̂(q0, ab) = {q2, q3}, so ab is accepted; the ε-free NFA keeps the same 4 states with final set F' = {q2, q3}.

traps: Forgetting the closure of the start state. If q0 has an ε-edge, read the first symbol from q0 and its ε-neighbours together.
Treating closure as symmetric. Follow arrow direction only.
Making a state final only if it was final before. A non-final state with an ε-path to a final state must become final.
Writing ε inside the string. Strings are over Σ only.
Dropping the closure after the move. The set produced by the symbol move is not closed, so always take ECLOSE of it. Move only from a closed set, which is why the run starts at ECLOSE(q0).

quiz.q: Write the transition function of an ε-NFA and name each part.
quiz.a: δ: Q × (Σ ∪ {ε}) → 2^Q. Q is the finite state set, Σ the alphabet, 2^Q the set of all subsets of Q, and the ε in the domain allows moves that read no input.
ECLOSE(q) is the set of all states reachable from q by a path of zero or more ε-edges. The zero-length path means q is always in its own closure.

quiz.q: Why do ε-edges give no extra computing power over plain NFAs?
quiz.a: Each ε-edge can be absorbed into moves on real symbols: set δ'(q, a) = δ̂(q, a) and make q final when its closure touches an old final state. The ε-free NFA accepts the same language, so the class stays the regular languages.

quiz.q: Explain why the closure of a set is the union of the closures of its members.
quiz.a: From any state in the set you may slide along ε-edges; different members reach different states and nothing else is reachable. So the reachable set is exactly the union.

quiz.q: An ε-NFA has q0 --ε--> q1, q1 --a--> q1, q1 --ε--> q2, q2 final. Find ECLOSE(q0) and decide whether the strings ε and a are accepted.
quiz.a: ECLOSE(q0) = {q0, q1, q2} because q1 reaches q2 by ε. So δ̂(q0, ε) contains q2: ε is accepted. On a: the a-move from q1 gives q1, closure {q1, q2}, which contains q2, so a is accepted.

quiz.q: For the machine in the figure, compute δ̂(q0, ba) and say whether ba is accepted.
quiz.a: Start {q0, q1}. Read b: b-moves are none from q0 and q2 from q1, union {q2}, closure {q2, q3}. Read a: a-moves are none from q2 and q3 from q3, union {q3}, closure {q3}. q3 is final, so ba is accepted.

quiz.q: A student deletes the two ε-edges from the figure's machine, keeps every symbol edge, and keeps F = {q3}. Which strings are now wrongly rejected, and what is the fix?
quiz.a: b and ab are wrongly rejected, because q0 can no longer slide to q1 before reading b, and q2 can no longer slide to q3. The fix is not only to change the finals: use δ'(q, a) = ECLOSE(δ(ECLOSE(q), a)) for every state and symbol, and set F' = {q | ECLOSE(q) ∩ F ≠ ∅}.

quiz.q: Two ε-NFAs accept the same language; one has 3 states and 5 ε-edges, the other 7 states and none. Which description is wrong, and what does that tell you about ε-edges?
quiz.a: Neither is wrong; both accept the same regular language. ε-edges are a description convenience that shortens machines, not a source of power, so questions about the language must be answered from the set of strings, not from the edge count.

beyond: Not for the exam. Lexer generators such as lex and flex turn regular expressions into ε-NFAs and then into a DFA by subset construction, and the generated scanner runs the DFA. Some newer libraries fall back to simulating the ε-NFA with state sets and closures when the DFA would grow too large, which saves memory on big rule sets. Search for 'Thompson construction' and 'RE2 automata library' to see production code that does exactly the closure step you did by hand. The same closure idea reappears for pushdown automata in Unit 4, where ε-moves change the stack without reading input.
